projects.title: First Rust programs
projects.description: Four small programs: a greeting that reads a name, then three functions that calculate with i32 and f64 values.

tasks.title: Greet someone by name
tasks.prompt:
The starter reads one line of input into `name` and trims the line break. Print exactly one line: `Hello, NAME! Welcome to Rust.` with the name in place of NAME.

If the input is `Ada`, the program prints `Hello, Ada! Welcome to Rust.`
hints: println! can print a variable by name inside the braces: `{name}`.
The whole line is `println!("Hello, {name}! Welcome to Rust.");`
tasks.correction: Compare your output with the expected line character by character. The comma, the exclamation mark and the full stop all count.
tasks.explanation: `let name = name.trim();` shadows the original `name` with the trimmed text, so the greeting has no stray line break. `{name}` inside the braces prints it.

cases.expected: Hello, Grace Hopper! Welcome to Rust.

tasks.title: Area of a rectangle
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `area` that returns the area of a rectangle. The width, the height and the result are all `i32` values.

The checker calls `area` for you, so this file needs no `fn main`. Run shows what your function returns for the example.
hints: The area is width multiplied by height.
Make `width * height` the last line of the body, with no semicolon.
tasks.correction: Check that the last line of the body is `width * height` with no semicolon after it. A semicolon would make the function return nothing.
tasks.explanation: The body's last expression is the return value, so `width * height` with no semicolon is returned as the `i32` the signature promises.

tasks.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
tasks.prompt:
Write `to_fahrenheit`, which takes a temperature in Celsius as an `f64` and returns it in Fahrenheit as an `f64`.

To convert, multiply by 9, divide by 5 and add 32. Every number in the calculation needs to be an `f64`, so write `9.0` rather than `9`.
hints: Rust won't multiply an f64 by the integer 9. Write the constants as 9.0, 5.0 and 32.0.
The formula is `celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0`.
tasks.correction: Check the order: multiply by 9.0, divide by 5.0, then add 32.0. Then check that the result is the last expression of the body, with no semicolon.
tasks.explanation: Every value in `celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0` is an `f64`, so Rust needs no conversion. Multiplication and division happen before the addition.

tasks.title: Average of three scores
tasks.prompt:
Write `average`, which takes three `i32` scores and returns their average as an `f64`.

The sum of three `i32` values is an `i32`. Convert it with `as f64` before dividing, or the remainder is lost.
hints: Add the three scores first. That sum is an i32.
`(a + b + c) as f64` gives you an f64. Divide it by 3.0.
tasks.correction: If you get a whole-number answer, the division happened between two i32 values. Convert the sum to f64 before dividing, and divide by 3.0.
tasks.explanation: `(a + b + c) as f64` converts the sum, then dividing by `3.0` keeps the fraction. Dividing first, with `(a + b + c) / 3`, would drop it.

projects.title: Text tools
projects.description: Four small functions that read text without copying it, using loops, slices and borrowed &str arguments: count the words, find the last one, shift letters and test for a palindrome.

tasks.title: Count the words in a line
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `count_words` that returns how many words a line of text holds. Words are separated by spaces, and extra spaces between them do not count as words.

The method `split_whitespace` gives the words one at a time, and `count` counts the items of an iterator.
hints: split_whitespace skips extra spaces, so you do not have to.
text.split_whitespace() is an iterator, and count() consumes it and returns the number of items.
tasks.correction: If a line with extra spaces gives the wrong number, check that you used split_whitespace and not split(' '), which makes an empty piece for each extra space.
tasks.explanation: split_whitespace gives only the real words, and count consumes the iterator and reports how many there were. An empty line has no words, so the result is 0.

tasks.title: The last word of a line
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `last_word` that returns the last word of a line as a slice of the input, without making a new String. An empty line has no last word, so return the empty text for it.

The iterator from `split_whitespace` has a method `last`, which returns an Option, and `unwrap_or("")` replaces a missing word with the empty text.
hints: text.split_whitespace().last() gives an Option<&str>.
Use unwrap_or("") on that Option for the case of an empty line.
tasks.correction: If the result has a leading or trailing space, check that you split on whitespace and did not slice the text yourself with a fixed index.
tasks.explanation: The words are slices of the original text, so nothing is copied. last returns None for an empty line, and unwrap_or supplies the empty text for that case.

tasks.title: Shift the letters of a text
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `shift_text` that moves every lowercase letter forward by `shift` places and wraps from z back to a. Other characters stay as they are. The shift is at most 25.

A character `c` can be turned into its place in the alphabet with `c as u8 - b'a'`, and a number back into a letter with `n as char`.
hints: Loop over text.chars(), and push each result onto a String made with String::new().
For a lowercase letter, the new place is (c as u8 - b'a' + shift) % 26, and adding b'a' turns it back into a byte.
Test c.is_ascii_lowercase() first, and push other characters unchanged.
tasks.correction: If a letter near the end of the alphabet comes out wrong, check that the remainder after dividing by 26 is taken before b'a' is added back.
tasks.explanation: The place of a letter is its distance from a. Adding the shift and taking the remainder after 26 wraps z back to a, and adding b'a' returns to the byte of a letter. Characters that are not lowercase letters are copied unchanged.

tasks.title: Does it read the same backwards
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `is_palindrome` that returns true when a text reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring upper and lower case.

The method `to_lowercase` returns a lowercase String, and `chars().rev()` walks the characters from the end.
hints: Make a lowercase copy first with text.to_lowercase().
Collect the characters forwards and backwards into two Vecs: lower.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>() and lower.chars().rev().collect::<Vec<char>>().
Two Vecs can be compared with ==.
tasks.correction: If Level and level disagree, check that you lowercased the text before comparing the two sequences.
tasks.explanation: Lowercasing makes the comparison ignore case. The two Vecs hold the same characters in opposite orders, and == on Vecs compares them item by item, so they are equal exactly when the text is a palindrome.

projects.title: Library catalogue
projects.description: A catalogue of books modelled with a struct and an enum for each book's state, an Option for lookups, a Result for checking a book out, and a HashMap for counting loans.

tasks.title: Model a book
tasks.prompt:
The program reads one line that says what state a book is in: `available`, `borrowed` followed by a name, or `lost`. Build a `Book` with the id 1 and the title Dune in that state, and print it with `{:?}`.

The types are written for you. Fill in `main` after the line is read.

For the input `borrowed ann` the program prints `Book { id: 1, title: "Dune", status: Borrowed("ann") }`.
hints: words.next() returns an Option<&str>, so you can match on it with Some("borrowed") and Some("lost") arms and a _ arm for the rest.
For borrowed, the member's name is the next word: words.next().unwrap_or("nobody").to_string().
Finish with let book = Book { id: 1, title: String::from("Dune"), status }; and println!("{:?}", book);
tasks.correction: Compare the printed line with the expected one exactly. The derive attribute gives the format, so a difference usually means that the wrong variant was built.
tasks.explanation: The match turns the first word into a Status variant, and the Borrowed variant carries the name that follows. Debug formatting, from the derive, prints the struct and its enum field without any further code.

tasks.title: Find a book by its id
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `title_for` that finds the title of the book with a given id. Ids start at 1, so id 1 is the first title in the slice. An id of 0, or one past the end, has no book, so return None for it.

The method `get` on a slice returns an Option<&&str>, and `copied()` turns that into an Option<&str>.
hints: Id 0 has no book, and subtracting 1 from a usize 0 would panic, so test for it first.
titles.get(id - 1) is an Option<&&str>. Add .copied() to get an Option<&str>.
tasks.correction: If id 0 stops the program with a panic, the check for 0 has to come before the subtraction.
tasks.explanation: get returns None for a position that does not exist, so ids past the end need no special case. Id 0 is handled first, because id - 1 would overflow, and the result is an Option, so the caller must decide what to do about a missing book.

tasks.title: Check out a book
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `checkout` that tries to lend a book to a member. The book's state is a text: `available`, `borrowed` followed by the holder's name, or `lost`.

If it is available, return Ok with the text `NAME has it now`. If it is borrowed, return Err with `already borrowed by HOLDER`. If it is lost, return Err with `lost`. For any other state, return Err with `no such book`.

The method `strip_prefix("borrowed ")` returns the rest of the text as an Option when it starts that way.
hints: Start with if state == "available", then use else if let Some(holder) = state.strip_prefix("borrowed ") for the second case.
format!("{member} has it now") builds the success text, and format!("already borrowed by {holder}") the failure.
Err needs a String, so write Err(String::from("lost")) or "lost".to_string().
tasks.correction: If one state gives the wrong message, check the order of the tests and that each failure is wrapped in Err.
tasks.explanation: The function says in its type that it can fail and what a failure looks like. Each branch returns exactly one of Ok or Err, and strip_prefix both tests the state and gives the holder's name.

tasks.title: Loans per member
tasks.prompt:
The input holds one member's name for every book that is out on loan, separated by whitespace. Count the loans for each member and print one line for each, in alphabetical order, in the form `NAME: COUNT`.

For the input `ann bo ann` the program prints `ann: 2` and then `bo: 1`.

The starter reads the whole input into `text`.
hints: Make a HashMap<&str, u32> and loop over text.split_whitespace().
*counts.entry(name).or_insert(0) += 1; counts one loan.
Collect the keys into a Vec, sort it, and print counts[*name] for each.
tasks.correction: A HashMap has no fixed order, so if the lines come out in a different order from the expected one, sort the names before printing.
tasks.explanation: The entry method starts a new name at 0 and adds one for each loan. The keys of a HashMap come in no fixed order, so they are sorted before printing and the report is the same on every run.

cases.stdin: bo ann bo cy ann bo

projects.title: Score report
projects.description: A wider version of the report program: parse score lines with Result, summarise entries and groups with a trait, pick the top scores with a generic function, and report averages with an iterator chain.

tasks.title: Parse one line of scores
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `parse_line` that turns a line such as `ann,8` into the name and the score. Spaces around either part are ignored.

If the line has no comma, return Err with `missing comma`. If the score is not a whole number, return Err with `bad score for NAME: ` followed by the message of the parse error.
hints: line.split_once(',') returns an Option of the two parts, and .ok_or("missing comma")? turns None into an Err.
score.trim().parse::<u32>() gives a Result, and .map_err(|e| format!("bad score for {}: {}", name.trim(), e))? changes its error into a String.
Finish with Ok((name.trim().to_string(), score)).
tasks.correction: If the message for a bad score is wrong, check that the format! text matches exactly and that map_err comes before the ?.
tasks.explanation: Each step that can fail ends in a question mark, so the first failure leaves the function with its Err and the later steps run only for good input. map_err puts every error into the one type that the function promises.

cases.expected: Err("bad score for cy: invalid digit found in string")

tasks.title: A Summary trait
tasks.prompt:
The starter defines `trait Summary` with one method, `summarise`, and two structs: `Entry` for one score and `Group` for all the scores of one name. Implement the trait for both.

For an Entry, `summarise` returns `NAME scored SCORE`. For a Group, it returns `NAME: AVERAGE (COUNT scores)`, with the average printed with one decimal place.

The program reads a line such as `ann 8 10`, and prints the summary of an Entry for the first score and then of the Group of all of them.
hints: Write impl Summary for Entry { fn summarise(&self) -> String { ... } } and the same for Group.
format!("{} scored {}", self.name, self.score) builds the text for an Entry.
For a Group, add the scores with self.scores.iter().sum::<u32>() as f64, divide by self.scores.len() as f64, and print the average with {:.1}.
tasks.correction: If the average is printed with too many decimals, add :.1 inside the braces. If the count is wrong, use self.scores.len().
tasks.explanation: The trait names one behaviour, and each type supplies its own body for it. main calls summarise in the same way on both, and each call runs the body that belongs to the value in front of the dot.

tasks.title: The top n of anything
tasks.prompt:
Write a generic function `top_n` that returns the `n` largest items of a slice, largest first, as a new Vec. If the slice has fewer than `n` items, return all of them.

It must work for any type that can be compared and cloned, so the bounds are `T: PartialOrd + Clone`.
hints: items.to_vec() makes a Vec that you may sort, and it needs Clone.
v.sort_by(|a, b| b.partial_cmp(a).unwrap()) sorts from largest to smallest.
v.truncate(n) keeps at most n items, and returns nothing, so return v on the next line.
tasks.correction: If the order is reversed, check that the closure compares b with a and not a with b. If the length is wrong, check truncate.
tasks.explanation: The bounds promise what the body uses: Clone for to_vec and PartialOrd for partial_cmp. Comparing b with a reverses the order, and truncate leaves the whole Vec alone when it holds fewer than n items.

tasks.title: Averages with a minimum
tasks.prompt:
Write a function `averages` that takes a slice of score lists, one list per person, and a minimum count. It returns the average of each list that has at least that many scores, in the same order.

Use an iterator chain with `filter`, `map` and `collect`. The closure given to `filter` is where the minimum is used.
hints: lists.iter().filter(|l| l.len() >= min) keeps the long enough lists, and the closure captures min.
map(|l| l.iter().sum::<u32>() as f64 / l.len() as f64) turns a list into its average.
End with .collect(), and the return type tells it to build a Vec<f64>.
tasks.correction: If a list that is too short appears in the result, check that the filter comes before the map. If a decimal is cut short, convert the sum with as f64 before dividing.
tasks.solution:
fn averages(lists: &[Vec<u32>], min: usize) -> Vec<f64> {
    lists
        .iter()
        .filter(|l| l.len() >= min)
        .map(|l| l.iter().sum::<u32>() as f64 / l.len() as f64)
        .collect()
}
tasks.explanation: The filter closure captures min from the function's parameters and keeps only the lists that are long enough. The map computes each average, and collect gathers them, so no loop or intermediate Vec is written.
